cards.title: Python runtime & object model
cards.summary: Interview-level mental model for names, objects, dynamic typing, duck typing, and what CPython actually executes.

entries.meaning: Types belong to objects rather than variable names, so the same name may later be rebound to an object of another type.
Assignment binds a name to an existing object; it does not copy that object unless you explicitly create a copy.
Code usually depends on the operations an object supports rather than requiring one exact declared class.
entries.detail: stream.read() works for any compatible object

entries.meaning: CPython compiles Python source to bytecode before executing it with the interpreter rather than executing source text directly line by line.
type() returns an object's runtime type and is useful for inspection, though polymorphic code often prefers capability checks or isinstance().
Check whether an object is an instance of a class or any subclass, which is usually safer than exact type equality.
None is a singleton sentinel for absence, so identity comparison is the conventional and reliable check.
Function parameters become local names bound to the caller's objects, so mutating a passed mutable object can be visible to the caller.

more.meaning: CPython may cache compiled bytecode in __pycache__ so unchanged modules do not need to be recompiled on every import.
A module's __name__ is its import name, while a directly executed module receives the special value __main__.
id() identifies an object for its lifetime in the current process and is useful for understanding aliasing, not business identity.
Implementation-level caching can make some equal strings or integers share identity, so never use is for ordinary value comparison.
more.detail: use a == b, not a is b

cards.title: Context managers
cards.summary: Use with to pair resource acquisition and guaranteed cleanup, including custom and generator-based context managers.

entries.meaning: Enter a managed resource for a block and guarantee its exit logic runs when the block finishes, including when an exception occurs.
entries.detail: with open(path) as f: data = f.read()

entries.meaning: Called when entering a with block; its return value becomes the object bound after as.
Called when leaving a with block with exception information when relevant, making it the cleanup hook for class-based managers.
Returning a truthy value from __exit__ tells Python that a raised exception was handled and should not propagate.
Create a context manager from one generator function instead of writing a class with __enter__ and __exit__ methods.
In a @contextmanager function, code before yield is setup and code after yield is teardown that resumes when the with block exits.
entries.detail: acquire(); try: yield obj; finally: release()

entries.meaning: Manage several resources in one with statement; cleanup occurs in reverse order of successful entry.
entries.detail: with open(a) as fa, open(b) as fb: ...

entries.meaning: Synchronization primitives such as threading.Lock are context managers, so with lock gives exception-safe acquire/release behavior.

more.meaning: Use asynchronous context managers when entering or leaving a resource requires awaiting asynchronous work.
Create an asynchronous context manager from an async generator using the same setup-yield-cleanup structure.
Dynamically combine an unknown or conditional number of context managers and cleanup callbacks into one managed stack.
contextlib.suppress intentionally ignores only the named exception types inside a small explicit block.
Wrap an object that only exposes close() so it can participate safely in a with statement.

cards.title: Decorators
cards.summary: Understand what @decorator syntax actually does, how wrappers and closures work, and how to preserve the wrapped function correctly.

entries.meaning: A decorator receives a function or class and returns the object that should replace it after definition.
Decorator syntax is assignment performed after the function is created; @trace means run = trace(run).
A typical function decorator returns an inner wrapper that adds behavior before or after calling the original function.
Copy important metadata and expose __wrapped__ so the decorated function still behaves well with docs, debugging, and introspection tools.
Generic wrappers normally accept and forward *args and **kwargs so they do not accidentally restrict the wrapped callable's signature.
A decorator that itself accepts configuration uses one extra function level: configuration → decorator → wrapper.
Stacked decorators apply from the function outward, so @a above @b produces a(b(function)).
The returned wrapper can keep access to variables from the enclosing decorator scope even after that outer function has returned.
entries.detail: def trace(func): def wrapper(): return func()

more.meaning: A decorator around an async function normally needs an async wrapper that awaits the original coroutine rather than returning it unintentionally.
more.detail: async def wrapper(*a, **kw): return await func(*a, **kw)

more.meaning: A class implementing __call__ can act as a stateful decorator when the decoration itself needs persistent configuration or counters.
A wrapper around an instance method receives self as part of its forwarded positional arguments just like the original method.
property, classmethod and staticmethod are decorators too; each transforms how a function is exposed through a class.
Decoration happens when the containing module or class body executes, not each time the decorated function is later called.
more.detail: import module  # decorators run during definition

cards.title: GIL, threads, processes & asyncio
cards.summary: Choose the concurrency model from the workload: I/O waiting, CPU work, shared memory, process isolation, or cooperative async I/O.

entries.meaning: Concurrency means tasks can make progress during overlapping time; parallelism means multiple tasks are literally executing at the same time.
entries.detail: asyncio = concurrency · processes = parallel CPU work

entries.meaning: In the default CPython build, the Global Interpreter Lock allows only one thread at a time to execute Python bytecode.
entries.detail: CPU-bound Python threads do not normally scale across cores

entries.meaning: Threads share one process and memory space, making them lightweight and useful when work spends most of its time waiting on blocking I/O.
Processes have separate interpreters and memory, so CPU-bound Python can run on multiple cores at the cost of higher startup and communication overhead.
One event loop cooperatively switches between coroutines at await points, making it efficient for many concurrent I/O operations without one thread per task.
entries.detail: await network_call() yields control to the loop

entries.meaning: When most time is spent waiting for network, files, databases, or external services, threads or asyncio can overlap that waiting effectively.
When most time is spent executing Python computations, processes are the usual default-build choice for true multi-core parallelism.
Shared mutable state can still be corrupted when operations interleave, so protect critical sections with synchronization rather than relying on the GIL.

more.meaning: Optional free-threaded CPython builds can disable the GIL and run Python threads in parallel; do not assume this mode is the default interpreter configuration.
Some C-backed libraries release the GIL during heavy work, so their threaded performance can differ from pure-Python CPU workloads.
more.detail: library behavior depends on its implementation

more.meaning: Use a managed pool when you need a bounded set of worker threads rather than creating and joining threads manually.
more.detail: with ThreadPoolExecutor() as ex: ex.map(fn, items)

more.meaning: Use a managed pool of worker processes for parallelizable CPU work when arguments and results can cross process boundaries.
more.detail: with ProcessPoolExecutor() as ex: ex.map(fn, items)

more.meaning: Offload one blocking synchronous function so it does not freeze the event loop while the rest of the async application keeps running.

cards.title: pytest fixtures & parametrization
cards.summary: The pytest mechanics most often discussed in automation interviews: dependency injection, yield teardown, scope, parametrization, and built-in fixtures.

entries.meaning: A test requests a fixture by naming it as a function argument; pytest resolves and executes the matching fixture before calling the test.
A normal fixture runs its setup code once for that fixture instance and returns the object that pytest passes into dependent tests or fixtures.
Code before yield is setup, the yielded value is injected into the test, and pytest resumes the fixture after the test finishes to run teardown.
Scope controls how long one fixture instance is reused: function, class, module, package, or session.
Fixtures can depend on other fixtures through their own parameters, letting pytest build the dependency graph in the required order.
An autouse fixture applies automatically within its scope even when tests do not name it explicitly; use it sparingly because dependencies become less visible.
Run one test function against multiple explicit data sets while pytest reports each case as a separate test invocation.
Assert that a specific operation raises an expected exception and optionally inspect the captured exception object.

more.meaning: Temporarily replace attributes, environment variables, dictionary entries, or paths and let pytest restore them automatically after the test.
Receive an isolated temporary pathlib.Path directory for filesystem tests without managing cleanup manually.
Capture logging records emitted during a test so assertions can inspect levels, messages, and logger names.
Attach metadata such as smoke, integration, or slow to tests so suites can select or configure groups explicitly.
Return a callable from a fixture when one test needs to create several independently configured objects while sharing setup logic.

cards.title: HTTP clients for automation
cards.summary: Practical HTTP patterns for API tests and helpers: parameters, JSON, sessions, status handling, timeouts, and sync/async clients.

entries.meaning: Make a synchronous HTTP request with the requests library and always provide an explicit timeout in automation code.
Pass query parameters as structured data instead of manually concatenating and escaping them into the URL.
Use the json argument to serialize a Python object as JSON and set the appropriate content type automatically.
Pass request headers explicitly for authentication, content negotiation, correlation IDs, or other protocol metadata.
Convert unsuccessful HTTP status responses into exceptions when a helper expects a successful request instead of silently continuing.
Decode a JSON response into Python values; still validate status, schema, and expected fields rather than assuming the body is correct.
Reuse cookies, headers, and pooled connections across related requests instead of creating fully independent top-level calls each time.
entries.detail: with requests.Session() as session: session.get(url, timeout=5)

entries.meaning: httpx provides a requests-like synchronous client with modern timeout and connection-pooling APIs and a matching asynchronous client.

more.meaning: Use the asynchronous client when the surrounding application or test helper is already async and many I/O operations should overlap.
more.detail: async with httpx.AsyncClient(timeout=5) as client: await client.get(url)

more.meaning: Prefer the client's structured authentication mechanisms when available rather than hand-building Authorization values repeatedly.
Sessions persist cookies across calls, which makes them useful for login flows and other stateful API interactions.
On failure, keep enough request/response context for diagnosis without logging secrets or sensitive payloads.
more.detail: status · URL · correlation ID · safe body excerpt

more.meaning: Keep raw HTTP mechanics in reusable client helpers so tests can express business intent and centralize timeout, auth, and error handling.
more.detail: api.create_user(data) instead of requests.post(...) in every test

cards.title: Timeout, polling & retry
cards.summary: Bound waiting explicitly: use deadlines, poll observable conditions, and retry only failures that can reasonably succeed later.

entries.meaning: Every operation that can block on an external dependency should have a finite timeout so a failure cannot hang the entire test or worker indefinitely.
Use time.monotonic for elapsed-time deadlines because wall-clock changes do not move it backward or forward unexpectedly.
Repeatedly check the actual condition you need until it becomes true or the overall deadline expires instead of sleeping once and hoping.
Limit retries by attempt count or deadline so a persistent failure is surfaced rather than converted into an infinite loop.
Retry failures that may genuinely recover, such as temporary network errors or selected server responses, not deterministic validation or assertion failures.
entries.detail: retry TimeoutError, not ValueError from bad test data

entries.meaning: Increase the delay between attempts to reduce pressure on a dependency that may already be overloaded or recovering.
Add randomness to retry delays so many workers do not all retry at the same instant and create another traffic spike.
When retries are exhausted, preserve the final exception and useful attempt diagnostics instead of raising an unrelated generic timeout with no cause.

more.meaning: Distinguish the timeout of one call from the total time allowed for all polling or retry attempts combined.
Before retrying a write operation, understand whether repeating it can duplicate side effects or whether the API provides an idempotency mechanism.
more.detail: POST payment may need an idempotency key

more.meaning: A fixed sleep always waits the full delay when the condition becomes ready early and still fails when the system occasionally needs longer.
Choose a reasonable interval that balances detection speed against unnecessary calls or load on the dependency.
more.detail: poll every 0.2–1.0s instead of a busy loop

more.meaning: Centralize retry behavior in the client/helper layer when possible so individual tests do not implement inconsistent hidden retry policies.

cards.title: Regular expressions
cards.summary: The re operations most useful in interviews and automation: search, full validation, extraction, replacement, compiled patterns, groups, and flags.

entries.meaning: Write regular-expression patterns as raw strings in most cases so Python string escaping does not compete with regex backslashes.
Find the first match anywhere in the string and return a match object or None when no match exists.
Attempt a match only at the beginning of the string; it does not require the pattern to consume the entire string.
Require the entire string to satisfy the pattern, which is usually clearer than manually anchoring validation patterns.
Return all non-overlapping matches as strings or tuples, useful when you need the complete set of extracted values at once.
Iterate lazily over match objects when you need positions, groups, or many matches without building one result list first.
Return text with matching regions replaced by a string or replacement function.
Create a reusable pattern object when the same expression is applied repeatedly or when storing a configured pattern improves readability.

more.meaning: Parentheses capture parts of a match so code can extract only the fields it needs from the larger matched text.
Give captured fields meaningful names when positional group numbers would make parsing logic difficult to read or maintain.
Quantifiers are greedy by default; adding ? makes them consume as little text as needed for the overall match to succeed.
Flags alter matching behavior, for example case-insensitive matching, multiline anchors, or dot matching newline characters.
Escape user-provided literal text before inserting it into a regex so special characters are not interpreted as pattern syntax.

cards.title: Virtual environments & packaging
cards.summary: The project-isolation and dependency-management commands expected in practical Python interviews and day-to-day automation work.

entries.meaning: Create a project-specific virtual environment with its own interpreter context and isolated site-packages directory.
Activation mainly adjusts the shell PATH so python and installed console scripts resolve to the environment; using the environment's interpreter directly also works.
Run pip through the intended Python interpreter so package installation goes to the environment you actually selected.
Install a declared set of dependencies from a requirements file rather than manually recreating the environment package by package.
Modern Python projects use pyproject.toml for build-system configuration, project metadata, dependencies, and tool-specific configuration.
Declare runtime package requirements as project metadata when the project is packaged rather than hiding them only in developer setup notes.
Use standardized pyproject dependency groups for development-only sets such as test or docs dependencies when your tooling supports them.
Install the current project so imports resolve through the working source tree while development changes remain immediately visible.

more.meaning: An __init__.py file defines a regular package and can expose package-level names; namespace packages can exist without one, but ordinary projects usually keep it explicit.
Inspect where an installed distribution came from and which version the current interpreter environment is using.
Ask pip to verify that installed package dependency requirements are internally consistent in the current environment.
Capture the currently installed environment as pinned requirement lines; treat it as a snapshot, not automatically as the ideal dependency-design source.
Virtual environments contain paths tied to where they were created, so recreate them after moving a project instead of treating .venv as a portable artifact.

cards.title: Memory management & profiling
cards.summary: Know the CPython memory model at interview depth, then measure CPU and memory behavior before attempting optimization.

entries.meaning: The default CPython build primarily tracks how many references point to ordinary objects and can usually reclaim them when that count reaches zero.
entries.detail: dropping the last reference usually releases an ordinary object promptly

entries.meaning: A separate garbage collector supplements reference counting by finding unreachable reference cycles whose members would otherwise keep one another alive.
entries.detail: two objects referencing each other can still be collected

entries.meaning: del removes a name, item, or attribute reference; it does not guarantee the underlying object is destroyed if other references still exist.
Trigger an explicit garbage-collection pass for diagnostic or unusual lifecycle needs; normal application code should rarely need to force collection.
Report the shallow size of one object itself; referenced child objects are not recursively included in that number.
Trace Python memory allocations and compare snapshots to locate where memory growth is being allocated.
Profile function calls and cumulative CPU time to locate actual hot paths before rewriting code based on intuition.
Measure a small code path repeatedly under a controlled harness when comparing micro-level implementation choices.

more.meaning: Generators produce values lazily and can reduce peak memory when the consumer does not need the entire result collection at once.
Slotted classes can reduce per-instance attribute-storage overhead when creating very large numbers of simple objects, but add design constraints.
A weak reference observes an object without keeping it alive, useful for caches and back-references whose existence should not control lifetime.
Optimize only after profiling identifies a meaningful bottleneck; readability changes made for imagined performance often add complexity without useful gain.
more.detail: profile → identify hot path → optimize → measure again

more.meaning: Caches improve speed by intentionally retaining references, so an unbounded cache can become a memory-growth problem even when no object is technically leaked.
more.detail: prefer bounded @lru_cache when the key space can grow indefinitely
